issues.legal_issue: A suit that in substance seeks to avoid an instrument is governed by the limitation period for cancellation when the plaintiff knew of the instrument.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership under an earlier sale deed and sought a declaration that a later registered sale deed did not bind her.
She had knowledge of the later deed when it was executed and registered.
The present suit was filed long after that knowledge; an earlier suit had been withdrawn with liberty to file afresh.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred by limitation because it was, in substance, a claim to avoid or cancel the later instrument and was not brought within the applicable period after the plaintiff knew of it.
issues.legal_principle: Article 59 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to a claim to cancel or set aside an instrument, with time running from when the plaintiff first becomes entitled to seek that relief and knows the relevant facts. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.instrument_avoidance_suit: The plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking relief that would avoid or cancel an instrument.
predicates.plaintiff_knew_of_instrument: The plaintiff knew of the instrument and the relevant basis for seeking to avoid it.
predicates.suit_filed_after_applicable_limit: The plaintiff filed the suit after the applicable limitation period had run from that knowledge.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff sues to avoid an instrument after knowing of it and files after the applicable limitation period, the suit is barred by limitation.

issues.legal_issue: A registered instrument remains binding unless it is avoided by a proper declaration, and merely pleading that it is void does not establish that it is void.
material_facts: The plaintiff argued that the later sale deed was void because it had been executed to stifle a prosecution and that she could seek only a declaration of ownership while remaining in possession.
The registered deed recited valuable consideration and the discharge of pre-existing debts.
No issue was raised, and no finding was made, that the deed was void under section 23 of the Contract Act; the plaintiff's pleading alone did not establish that claim.
issues.conclusion: The court rejected the argument that the plaintiff could avoid the deed without seeking its avoidance or cancellation. Until avoided by a proper declaration, the duly registered deed remained valid and binding.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Evidence Act barred oral evidence contradicting the deed's recitals. Section 23 of the Contract Act was not a basis for treating the deed as void because no issue or finding to that effect existed; pleading alone was insufficient. A duly registered instrument remains valid and binding until avoided by proper declaration. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenging_registered_instrument and instrument_is_registered and invalidity_is_only_pleaded and instrument_not_avoided_by_court

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_registered_instru: A party brought a civil suit challenging the effect or validity of an instrument.
predicates.invalidity_is_only_pleaded: The party alleged that the instrument was invalid, but the allegation was not established by an adjudication that it was void.
predicates.instrument_not_avoided_by_court: A court had not avoided or cancelled the instrument by a proper declaration.

issues.definition: When a registered instrument is challenged in a civil suit but invalidity is only alleged and no court has avoided it, the instrument remains binding until avoided.
